title: 1  A World of Fat Tails
text:
Additive randomness and the Gaussian
I have written roughly forty grant proposals in the past six years, as the CTO at Irradiant. Most were for Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) grants, the federal program that funds early technical work at small companies, each asking for a few hundred thousand dollars. Every proposal takes weeks of trying to cram all of the technical detail into the page limit, making all of the budget justification numbers line up across different documents, tracking down letters of support, and always the final push wrestling with the government submission portal. All of this for some small chance of maybe getting the opportunity to get paid to do the work I really wanted to be doing.
In the moment, I always end up asking myself: is it worth it? There is a huge range in the amount of money that grants can provide. Typical Phase I SBIR grants bring in a few hundred thousand dollars, while a Phase II is often one or two million. Winning even a half dozen of these is months of effort for a few million dollars, which is not bad. But that total amount from multiple grants can then be dwarfed by a single DARPA program bringing in over $10M, even though the effort of writing that one large proposal is far less than writing six smaller proposals. Even larger R&D grant opportunities are rarer, but can reach tens to hundreds of millions. For me, the single DARPA program made up the large majority of every award I was a part of winning. That one definitely felt worth the late nights. Does that mean all of the others were a waste of time?
Is there a way of understanding, maybe even trying to predict, these kinds of opportunities? Given limited time and resources, how do we, as founders, decide where to focus our efforts, or make decisions around what is worth pursuing? If we make a series of bets, whether that’s grant proposals, or sales pitches, or VC meetings, what kind of payoff can we expect? How do we think about our odds of surviving, or even, maybe, thriving? To start even thinking about these kinds of questions, we need to have some understanding of probability and statistics beyond the everyday.
The tallest man ever measured stood 2.72 m, about 1.6 times the height of an average adult. If you met a thousand strangers and added up their heights, the tallest of them would contribute a little more than a thousandth of the total. If you had to estimate the average human height, no one you see on the street will make you think that you are radically far from the truth. This is the world of Gaussian statistics.
Now try the same exercise with companies. The largest firms in an economy have millions of times the revenue of the median firm. If you picked a thousand startups at random, a handful would account for most of the combined value and the rest would be rounding error. Meeting one more company can change your estimate of the average, by a lot. This is the world of fat-tailed statistics, a world brought to popular attention by Nassim Taleb in his book The Black Swan. In Figure 1.1 you can see that the number of US companies with at least a certain number of employees is well-fit by a power law over six orders of magnitude. If human heights followed the same distribution, the tallest person would be millions of meters tall, about ten times taller than the Earth’s atmosphere.
These are two fundamentally different worlds, and the second is the one we live in as founders. In this chapter we will explore why each of these kinds of statistics show up so frequently, and under what conditions. Then we will set out some of the consequences that the rest of this book explores.
Take a quantity that is the sum of many small independent contributions, none of which dominates:
X = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \cdots + \varepsilon_n .
The central limit theorem says that whatever the distribution of the individual terms (provided each has finite variance), the sum approaches a Gaussian. That is, each contribution \varepsilon_i could be a uniform distribution like a die roll, or itself a Gaussian distribution, or something lopsided like the exponential distribution of waiting times between radioactive decays, and when you add many of them together, you get a Gaussian distribution out. Thermal noise in a resistor, the position of a diffusing particle, and the error of a carefully repeated measurement are all sums of this kind. So is adult height, which depends on many genes and environmental effects of small, roughly additive size.
The feature of the Gaussian that we will focus on is the speed at which its tails die. This tells you how likely it is to see a really extreme outcome. Mathematically, the probability of landing more than z standard deviations above the mean falls like e^{-z^2/2}:
\Pr(Z > z) \approx \frac{\varphi(z)}{z} = \frac{1}{z\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-z^2/2} \quad \text{for large } z .
A 3σ event (meaning an event three standard deviations from the mean) happens about once in 740 draws, a 5σ event once in 3.5 million, and a 10σ event has probability 10^{-23}. For practical purposes the distribution has a hard edge a few standard deviations out. This has some implications. One, mentioned at the beginning, is that the sample mean is stable. As you draw more and more samples, or take more and more measurements, you’re not going to get a result that fundamentally shifts the mean. This is also why outliers in an experiment can reasonably be thrown away as instrument faults, since you can safely assume that a wildly divergent measurement is some sort of fluke, and not meaningful data.

title: 1  A World of Fat Tails
text:
Multiplicative randomness and the log-normal
Now take a quantity that is a product of many uncertain factors:

X = f_1 \times f_2 \times \cdots \times f_n .

These kinds of quantities occur frequently. In a company, next year’s revenue is a product of this kind: the number of prospects reached, times the fraction who respond, times the fraction who buy, times the price, times how long they stay. The time to finish a task is another: the base estimate, times a factor for the thing you forgot, times a factor for the supplier who was late. Growth is a product by definition, since each year multiplies the last.
Take the logarithm and the product becomes a sum:

\ln X = \ln f_1 + \ln f_2 + \cdots + \ln f_n ,

so the central limit theorem applies to \ln X. The logarithm is thus Gaussian, and X itself is log-normal. If \ln X has mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma, then

\text{median} = e^{\mu}, \qquad \text{mean} = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}, \qquad \text{mode} = e^{\mu - \sigma^2} .

The three measures of “typical” (mean, median, and mode), which are the same in a Gaussian distribution, become separated in the log-normal distribution. The specific degree of separation is determined by \sigma alone. The mode is below the median by a factor e^{\sigma^2/2}, while the mean is above it by the same factor. Here \sigma is dimensionless: it measures uncertainty in multiplicative factors. A \sigma of 0.1 means “known to about ±10%,” and the distribution is nearly Gaussian. A \sigma of 1 means “typically off by a factor of 2.7 either way,” and the distribution is strongly skewed. At \sigma = 2, the log-normal distribution is even more skewed. At this level, five outcomes out of six are below average, and one draw in a hundred holds more than a third of everything. As \sigma increases, more and more weight of the overall distribution is held in the “tail”, meaning very unlikely events have very large impact. This is the origin of the term “fat-tailed.”

title: 1  A World of Fat Tails
text:
Power laws
A third family has tails that are heavier still. A power-law (or Pareto) distribution has

\Pr(X > x) = \left(\frac{x_{\min}}{x}\right)^{\alpha} \quad \text{for } x \ge x_{\min} .

The exponent \alpha is called the tail index. Smaller \alpha means a fatter tail. The distribution has no characteristic scale: the chance of exceeding 2x, given that you have exceeded x, is 2^{-\alpha} no matter how large x already is. A company that has reached $10 million in revenue has the same odds of reaching $20 million as a company at $100 million has of reaching $200 million.
Power laws arise from a few generic mechanisms. One is rich get richer: when the growth of a thing is proportional to its current size, and new things keep entering at the bottom, the stationary distribution of sizes is a power law. City populations, citation counts, and firm sizes all behave this way. Another is multiplicative growth with a floor, where the floor keeps the distribution from drifting to zero and a power-law tail develops above it. City sizes are a well-studied case: each city grows or shrinks by a random percentage each year, but a town that shrinks far enough stops being counted as a city, and the economist Xavier Gabaix showed that this alone produces the power law seen in city populations. Firms are similar, since a company’s headcount changes by percentages but cannot fall below one person; it closes instead. A third mechanism to generate a power law is a mixture: log-normals with a spread of different \sigma values produce a tail that is hard to tell from a power law. Startup outcomes pooled across industries are a plausible example. Within one sector, outcomes may be roughly log-normal, but software, biotech and restaurants have very different spreads, and the pooled distribution has a heavier tail than any single sector’s.
The moments of a power law are where intuition fails. The mean is finite only when \alpha > 1, and then equals \alpha\, x_{\min}/(\alpha - 1). The variance is finite only when \alpha > 2. Many of the quantities this book cares about have a tail index between 1 and 2: a finite mean and an infinite variance. For such a quantity the sample standard deviation does not converge to anything. It simply grows with the size of the largest observation you happen to have seen.
The famous 80/20 rule, that 80% of completion is achieved with 20% of the time or effort, is a statement about \alpha. In a Pareto distribution the top fraction p of draws holds a share p^{\,1 - 1/\alpha} of the total. Setting the top 20% to hold 80% gives \alpha = \ln 5 / \ln 4 \approx 1.16. With that same exponent, the top 1% hold 53%.
I first learned about the 80/20 rule in college at Olin. Olin uses a project-based approach to engineering education, so that instead of weekly problem sets, most classes would involve several longer-term projects. Problem sets, which are curated in advance, tend to take a relatively consistent amount of time, and require a roughly consistent amount of effort for each problem. That is, they are more Gaussian in nature. Projects, in contrast, have fatter tails, and so the 80/20 rule applies. The problem, of course, is that it’s often not known in advance which 80% of a project will take 20% of the effort, versus which 20% will take 80%. This applies directly to you as a founder, since starting a company looks a lot more like a project (or a series of projects) than like a curated problem set, with the corresponding importance of log-normal or Pareto distributions. The implications of this will be explored in chapter 10.

Lab 1.1: Guess the Distribution. Each round draws numbers from a hidden distribution: a Gaussian, a log-normal, or a power law with \alpha < 2. Look at the raw values and the histogram, then name the family. Start with 20 points, then see how many you need before you can tell reliably.



Things to try

Play five rounds at 20 points without the summary statistics. How often can you tell a log-normal from a power law?
For a sample you got wrong, raise the number of points to 1,000. Which feature of the data gives the answer away?
Switch on logarithmic bins. A log-normal turns into a symmetric bell on that scale, while a power law keeps a long right-hand tail.
Turn on the summary statistics and watch “largest value ÷ median” as you add points. For a Gaussian it barely moves; for a power law it keeps growing.

title: 1  A World of Fat Tails
text:
Rare events








Figure 1.2: Probability of exceeding x for three distributions with the same median, on logarithmic axes. The power law is a straight line whose slope is −α. The log-normal is a parabola that bends away slowly. The Gaussian (standard deviation equal to half the median) is gone before x reaches 5.



Figure 1.2 illustrates the key practical difference between the Gaussian world and the world of fat-tails. It plots the probability of exceeding a value x, where x is expressed in multiples of the median of the distribution. Consider the probabilities of seeing a few extreme values: the chance of an outcome more than ten times the median is 1% for this log-normal and 3.5% for this power law. For the Gaussian it is 10^{-72}, a number so small it has no physical meaning and is essentially zero. Said another way, for a value that you will never in the age of the universe observe from a Gaussian distribution, you will see from fat-tailed distributions in more than one in a hundred observations.
Going even more extreme, at a hundred times the median, the log-normal gives two in a million and the power law still gives one in 400. Remember that all three distributions have the same median, so in the middle of the distribution, where most of your data will be, they are hard to tell apart. And yet, in the tail, they differ by astronomical amounts. That is what it means to be fat-tailed.
Plotting data in this way can be useful to distinguish between distributions. If you plot the fraction of observations exceeding x against x on log-log paper and you see a cliff, that means thin tails. A straight line or a gentle curve that keeps going means fat tails. Distinguishing a log-normal from a power law takes a great deal of data and is rarely worth the effort, because the decisions they imply are the same. Below we outline some of the consequences of this fat-tailed behavior, which will come up again and again in this book, and in your journey as a founder.

title: 1  A World of Fat Tails
section: Consequence 1: calculating the average from data doesn’t work
text:
Consequence 1: calculating the average from data doesn’t work
Everyone knows that you want more data to be able to calculate more reliable statistics. When doing an experiment, you make sure to repeat your experiment a reasonable number of times, calculate the average result, and use that. This makes a lot of sense in a Gaussian world, where the mean of n observations converges on the true mean with an error that shrinks as n^{-1/2}. Four times the data halves the error, and generally more data monotonically leads to a better estimate of the average. If you get one wildly off measurement that skews the whole average, you discard that as an outlier.
This intuition falls apart in the fat-tailed world. For a power law with 1 < \alpha < 2 the sample mean still converges, but its error shrinks only as n^{-(1 - 1/\alpha)}. At \alpha = 1.5 that is n^{-1/3}, so halving the error takes eight times the data. At \alpha = 1.16, where the 80/20 rule applies, the exponent is 0.14, and halving the error takes about 150 times the data. In the startup world, data you might want to get includes customer interest, product-market fit, whether a business model is profitable, how long it typically takes to create a new product, or whether a potential hire will be productive. These are generally not areas where it is possible to get anywhere close to 100 data points.
The situation is even worse for \alpha<1. In this case, the average is undefined. As you take more and more data, the average diverges more and more.








Figure 1.3: Running average of the first n observations, for three independent runs of each distribution. Left: both distributions have a true mean of 1. The Gaussian averages settle within a few hundred draws. The power-law averages sit below the truth for long stretches and then jump when a large value arrives. Right: a power law with \alpha = 0.8 has no finite mean. The running average never settles; it climbs roughly as n^{0.25}, about tenfold for every ten-thousandfold increase in data, with each new record pulling it higher.



Figure 1.3 shows what that looks like. The Gaussian runs wobble for a few dozen observations and then settle into the true mean. The power-law runs behave differently in kind. For long stretches the running average drifts below the true mean, because the rare large values that hold much of the mass have not shown up yet. Then one arrives and the average jumps. After a thousand observations the three runs still disagree by tens of percent. The right-hand panel shows the \alpha < 1 case, where there is no true value to converge on at all.
Two important lessons follow directly from these behaviors. First, in a fat-tailed world your experience is biased toward optimism about risk, and pessimism about reward. Because most samples do not contain the rare events that dominate the mean, using past data to try to predict the future will lead you to underestimate the potential for large future changes, good or bad. A founder who has closed twenty small deals (or won twenty small grants) has learned very little about what the average deal will be once a large one lands.
Second, an error bar computed from a small fat-tailed sample should be read as a lower bound on your ignorance. In practice, when dealing with a fat-tailed distribution, as you take more samples you should expect your observed variation to grow. This is a result of hitting those rarer-but-larger events.
This does not make past data or averages useless. Means still add: the expected total of ten deals is ten times the expected deal, whatever the distribution. That fact drives chapter 10, where the mean and the median of a task’s duration turn out to be different numbers and a schedule built from medians is late almost every time. For a fat-tailed quantity, the mean is still a very useful piece of information to have, but getting an accurate estimate of the average becomes much, much more difficult than what you expect if you are used to the Gaussian world.

title: 1  A World of Fat Tails
section: Consequence 2: the past is a poor bound on the future
text:
Consequence 2: the past is a poor bound on the future
For a Gaussian, the largest of n observations grows like \sqrt{2 \ln n} standard deviations, which is so slow that it hardly matters. A thousand observations reach about 3.2σ and a million reach about 4.9σ. The largest value you have seen is a decent guide to the largest you will see.
For a power law the largest of n observations grows like n^{1/\alpha}. With \alpha = 1.5, ten times as much experience brings a maximum 4.6 times as large. The record is always waiting to be broken by a wide margin, and the worst delay, the biggest customer and the most expensive mistake in your history say little about the next ones. If you develop a plan for the future based on “the worst case we have seen,” then that plan has been tested against a number that fat-tailed statistics promise will be exceeded. Always keep in mind the possible “Black Swan” events.

title: 1  A World of Fat Tails
section: Consequence 3: only a few big things matter
text:
Consequence 3: only a few big things matter








Figure 1.4: Share of the total held by the largest 1% of draws. For a Gaussian quantity whose spread is 20% of its mean, the top 1% hold 1.5% of the total. For the 80/20 power law they hold more than half.



In a thin-tailed world the total is made of many comparable contributions. In a fat-tailed world it is made of a few large ones plus a crowd that hardly registers (Figure 1.4). In simulations of a thousand draws, the single largest value is typically 0.16% of the total for the Gaussian, about 5% for a power law with \alpha = 1.5, and about 11% for the 80/20 power law. In about one run in twenty it is more than half.
This is possibly the most practical lesson in this book. If the value of your customers is fat-tailed, then most of your revenue will come from a few of them, and your most important job is to find and keep those few. If the value of your tasks is fat-tailed, then most of what you accomplish in a year will come from a handful of days. If investor returns are fat-tailed, then an investor’s whole fund depends on one or two companies, which explains a good deal about how investors behave, something we will explore more in chapter 2.
This characteristic of fat-tailed distributions also changes what counts as an error. In a thin-tailed world, being 10% wrong on everything costs you 10%. In a fat-tailed world, you can be wrong about almost everything and it will not matter, provided you are right about the few items that carry the total. Literally, don’t sweat the small stuff. Precision spread evenly is wasted effort. Chapter 6 develops this into a rule for where to spend measurement effort.

title: 1  A World of Fat Tails
text:
Which world are you in?
You rarely have enough data to fit a distribution, so often it can be better to judge by mechanism. Ask yourself these four questions:

Is the quantity a sum or a product? Sums of comparable terms are thin-tailed. Products, growth processes and anything with compounding are fat-tailed.
Is there a physical bound? A person cannot work 500 hours in a week or weigh a tonne. Bounded quantities are thin-tailed. Revenue, valuations, downloads and delays have no ceiling of that kind.
Could one observation outweigh all the others combined? If the answer is plainly no, relax. If it is “that happens all the time,” you are in the fat-tailed world.
Does success feed itself? Network effects, reputation, word of mouth and reinvested profit are all rich-get-richer mechanisms and all produce power laws.








Usually thin-tailed
Usually fat-tailed




Monthly payroll and rent
Outcome of a company, a product or a funding round


Unit manufacturing cost in a stable process
Revenue per customer, deal size


Time for a task you have done fifty times
Time for a task you have never done


Measurement error on a calibrated instrument
Cost of a defect that reaches a customer


Number of hours you work in a week
Value produced by one of those hours


Attendance at the weekly meeting
Impact of a single hire, idea or introduction



The left column is where spreadsheets, averages and error bars behave nicely. The right column is where most of the important things in a startup live, and where we will focus our attention for the rest of this book.






TipKey idea



Before reasoning about any uncertain quantity, ask whether its randomness multiplies, or ask if there are “rich-get-richer” feedback mechanisms. If so, put yourself in the fat-tailed mindset: think in factors and logarithms, describe it with quantiles, and expect the total to be dominated by a few draws.



Lab 1.2: Tail Explorer. Draw samples from a Gaussian, a log-normal and a power law with adjustable tail weight. Watch the running average, the largest draw and the share held by the top 1% as the sample grows, then resample and see how much the answers move.
Draw a sample from one of three families and watch the statistics you would normally trust. The Gaussian has mean 1. The log-normal has median 1 and a spread \sigma in its logarithm. The power law has \Pr(X > x) = x^{-\alpha} for x \ge 1. The tail-weight slider moves \sigma from 0.2 to 2.5, or \alpha from 3 down to 1.05.



Things to try

Select the power law at a tail weight near 0.95 (\alpha \approx 1.15, the 80/20 case). Draw new samples several times and watch “sample mean ÷ true mean”. How often is it below 1?
Keep the same setting and raise the number of draws from 100 to 100,000. Does the largest draw’s share of the total shrink the way it would for a Gaussian?
Switch to the Gaussian. Nothing you do with the sliders will make the top 1% hold more than a few percent.
Find the log-normal \sigma at which the top 1% of draws hold a quarter of the total.

text:
Further reading

M. E. J. Newman, Power laws, Pareto distributions and Zipf’s law (2005). The best single review for a physicist, with the generating mechanisms worked out.
A. Clauset, C. R. Shalizi and M. E. J. Newman, Power-law distributions in empirical data (2009). How to test for a power law properly, and how often published claims fail the test.
N. N. Taleb, Statistical Consequences of Fat Tails (2020). Technical and opinionated. The first few chapters cover why standard estimators fail.
M. Mitzenmacher, A brief history of generative models for power law and lognormal distributions, Internet Mathematics (2004). Shows how small changes in a multiplicative process move you between the two families.
X. Gabaix, Zipf’s law for cities: an explanation, Quarterly Journal of Economics (1999). Random percentage growth with a lower bound produces a power law.
US Census Bureau, Statistics of U.S. Businesses. Annual counts of firms by employment size, the source for the firm-size figure.
R. L. Axtell, Zipf distribution of U.S. firm sizes, Science (2001). The evidence that firm sizes follow a power law with an exponent close to 1.

1  A World of Fat Tails

title: 2  Shots on Goal
text:
Startup returns are fat-tailed
Chapter 1 argued that company outcomes belong to the fat-tailed world. This fact is at the foundation of the VC funding model, which we will start exploring here. Recall that in a fat-tailed world, a small number of outcomes dominates the overall result. VCs take advantage of this by making a variety of bets, knowing that many will fail, but only the few successes really matter. You, as a founder with only one company, are perhaps not so wise. Or are you? In this chapter we will arrive at four rules for a founder. The chapter ends with an uncomfortable corollary about how little a single outcome can teach you.
A financing is one investment round in one company, and its return multiple is the money eventually returned to those investors divided by the money they put in. Correlation Ventures, a venture firm, compiled the multiples for more than 21,000 financings of US startups between 2004 and 2013.
About 65% of financings returned less than the amount invested. About 4% returned ten times or more, and 0.4% returned fifty times or more. Note that these are companies that had already convinced professional investors to fund them, so the high return outcomes are even more rare if you count all of the companies that failed before even getting funding.
The counts in Figure 2.1 also understate the skew in dollar terms, because a 50× winner gets lumped in with 500× winners. Horsley Bridge, an investor in many venture funds, shared three decades of data with the firm Andreessen Horowitz: about 6% of investments produced about 60% of all the returns. In 2012 Paul Graham wrote that two companies accounted for roughly three-quarters of the combined value of everything the accelerator Y Combinator had funded up to then. That’s two out of about 400 companies accounting for a large majority of the total value.
Clearly, venture-backed startup outcomes are fat-tailed. These numbers are what the 80/20 power law of chapter 1 looks like in dollars.

2  Shots on Goal

title: 2  Shots on Goal
section: How investors respond, and why you should care
text:
How investors respond, and why you should care
VC investors know that they are getting returns from a fat-tailed distribution, and much of their mindset and behavior is explained accordingly. A venture fund typically holds a portfolio: twenty to forty companies bought with one pool of money. If 6% of investments produce 60% of the returns, the entire fund’s result depends on whether it happens to hold the one or two outliers. Everything else, the other couple dozen startups, is noise.
Three behaviors follow from this situation, and each one affects you as a founder directly:
First, investors select for the size of the best case, far more than for the probability of success. An investor’s question when evaluating a company is always “if this works, can it return my whole fund?” A company with an 80% chance of becoming a solid business worth $60 million is, for a $200 million fund, a worse investment than one with a 5% chance of being worth $1 billion. In both cases, the expected value is around $50 million. For the former business, if the fund owns 20%, it ends up with around $12 million, which is noise compared to the total fund size. For the other business, success returns $200 million, thereby returning the fund. Chris Dixon called this the Babe Ruth effect, after the baseball player who led the league in both home runs and strikeouts: the best funds in the Horsley Bridge data lost money on more of their investments than mediocre funds did, striking out more often, but then made it back on the size of their hits. In the world of fat tails, a small number of results dominate.
Before moving on, consider what world you want to live in. You might be devoting the next ten or more years of your life to starting a company. Would you rather put that bet on the company with an 80% chance of being worth $60 million and a 20% chance of being worth nothing, or the one with a 5% chance of $1 billion and 95% chance of nothing?
After investing, the VCs will push you toward variance. A strategy that raises both the chance of failure and the size of the best case can be attractive to someone who holds thirty companies, but highly unattractive to a founder who holds one. This is a real conflict of interest, and it is structural. We will explore this more in chapter 3.
Your investors will not care if you are mildly successful. A company that is growing steadily toward a modest outcome lands in that 80%-chance-of-$60-million regime. For you, this could be great, but for the investor, it costs them the time it takes to sit on the board, and promises a negligible reward. If your honest ambition is a profitable $10 million business, venture capital is the wrong fuel, and the kindest thing you can do for everyone involved is to work that out before you take the money.
While these statistics may often put the incentives of investors and founders at odds, as founders there are also important lessons we can take away from the VC mindset.

title: 2  Shots on Goal
section: Rule 1: create convex bets and then maximize variance
text:
Rule 1: create convex bets and then maximize variance
A key feature of many fat-tailed distributions is that the variance is very large, and for power-law distributions with \alpha<2 it is infinite. When you can make the way your payoff depends on a distribution convex, then that large variance works to your advantage.
You can think of a payoff as a combination of the uncertain outcome of the outside world, X, and some payoff function f(X) that you have some control over. For example, X might be the value of a project, and f(X) could represent how you choose to pursue that project. The value of the project is probably fat-tailed, and could be highly negative (e.g., a project that goes far over budget without being successful), or highly positive (e.g., a project that is easier than expected and creates a new product that becomes the primary revenue driver for the whole company). Going into the project, you don’t know which way it will go. A sensible person would likely not fully commit to the project right from the start. Instead, you may want to do a lower-cost initial prototype, learn cheaply whether a good or bad outcome is more likely, and then choose whether to pursue the project or drop it. This is one method of making your payoff convex.
A function f(X) on an interval is convex if, for any two points on its graph, the straight line segment (chord) connecting them lies on or above the graph between them. This is true when the function’s slope never decreases as X increases, which is the case whenever its second derivative is positive. A useful example of a convex bet is an option: a small, known cost now that buys the right, but not the obligation, to make a larger commitment later, once you know more. Sending a cold email to a dream customer, a cheap option on a patent, and building a two-week prototype for a new application are convex in this way: the worst case is a known, small cost, and if the result looks promising, meaning more likely to end up with a fat-tail result, then you invest further, while if it doesn’t, then you walk away. A payoff is concave when the gains are capped and the losses are open: a fixed-price development contract where costs could overrun indefinitely, a personal guarantee on a company loan, or skipping a safety review to save a week.
For a convex payoff, uncertainty is an asset. This is expressed by Jensen’s inequality, which says that the expected value of your convex payoff is larger than the payoff that results from the average outcome. Mathematically, if f, the payoff you get from a particular random outcome X, is convex, then \mathbb{E}[f(X)] \ge f(\mathbb{E}[X]), and the gap between \mathbb{E}[f(X)] and f(\mathbb{E}[X]) widens with the spread of X. Some examples of this are shown in Figure 2.2.








Figure 2.2: Jensen’s inequality, drawn. In each panel the outcome X is equally likely to land at either end of the dashed chord, so the average payoff \mathbb{E}[f(X)] is the chord’s midpoint, while the payoff from the average outcome, f(\mathbb{E}[X]), sits on the curve directly below or above it. The solid vertical segment is the gap. For a convex payoff the chord lies above the curve and the gap favors uncertainty; for a concave payoff it lies below and uncertainty costs you. Widening the spread of X widens the gap. An option is convex only through its kink at K, yet that is enough: averaging a loss avoided with a gain kept beats the zero you get from the average outcome.



A worked case shows the size of the effect. Suppose a project would cost K to carry out and would turn out to be worth X, where X is log-normal with mean equal to K, so committing to it blind only breaks even on average. Now suppose a cheap experiment, such as a prototype or a pilot, tells you X before you commit, and you go ahead only when X > K. The value of that right to choose is

\mathbb{E}\big[\max(X - K,\, 0)\big] = K\left[\,2\,\Phi\!\left(\tfrac{\sigma}{2}\right) - 1\right] ,

which is zero when there is no uncertainty and rises steadily with \sigma, the standard deviation of \ln X. If the experiment costs less than this, it is worth running, and it is worth more the less you know.








Figure 2.3: A project whose average value only equals its cost K. As uncertainty grows, the median project is worth less and the chance that it would lose money rises above 80%, yet the value of being able to check first and walk away keeps climbing.



Figure 2.3 contains the central tension of entrepreneurship. Moving right, the typical project gets worse: at \sigma = 2 the median project is worth 14% of its cost, and 84% of such projects would lose money if you committed to them blind. The value of the option gets better: 0.20K at \sigma = 0.5, 0.38K at \sigma = 1 and 0.68K at \sigma = 2. Both statements are true together. A project can be more likely to fail and an option on it more valuable, provided finding out is sufficiently cheap.
Equity in a company is itself a convex instrument, because shareholders cannot lose more than they invested, but the value of the company can grow quite large. So, by founding a company, you are already making a convex bet. Now also think about it from an investor’s point of view. You may think that your company needs an investment of $100 million over five years to become a billion dollar company. However, you are not going to go out from day one and ask investors to put in $100 million. Generally investing happens in stages, such as Seed, Series A, Series B, etc. This allows investors to make smaller bets, often with pro rata rights that allow them to invest more in future rounds, and then wait to see if the startup is hitting an inflection point and maintaining the potential for a very large outcome. If not, they stop investing and lose a small amount that ends up being noise when compared to the fat-tail winners.
The practical implication of Jensen’s inequality is that when you are making a convex bet, more variance is to your advantage. We saw this already in the VC math, where a small chance of a billion-dollar company is far more valuable than a near-certain but small outcome. Turn this to your advantage by sorting every decision by the shape of its payoff. Collect cheap bets with capped downside and open upside. When the upside is open, aim as big as you can. The converse is true when the upside is capped but the downside is open. No matter the expected value, be very careful if the downside is open, and try to minimize the variance.

title: 2  Shots on Goal
section: Rule 2: the number of draws is the lever you control
text:
Rule 2: the number of draws is the lever you control
You cannot choose the outcome of a draw from a fat-tailed distribution, and by its nature you can expect most draws to be below average. What you can choose how many draws you take. If each attempt has an independent probability p of a large success, the chance of at least one in n attempts is 1 - (1-p)^n. With p = 5\% that is 5% for one attempt, 40% for ten and 79% for thirty.
In terms of your end payoff, the size of the best result matters as much as its probability. This is where the difference between the thin-tailed and fat-tailed worlds is stark.








Figure 2.4: Typical best result out of n independent attempts, where the median attempt is worth 1. With thin tails, extra attempts buy almost nothing. With fat tails, the best result keeps growing with n. The log-normal and power-law curves cross: with few attempts the log-normal does better, with many the power law does.



In a thin-tailed world, trying a thousand times instead of ten improves your best result from 1.45 to 1.96 times the median (Figure 2.4). In the log-normal world it goes from 9.5 to 121, and in the power-law world from 5.7 to 291. From the thin-tailed perspective, repeated attempts are clearly wasteful. When you are drawing from a fat-tailed set of outcomes, each new draw can dramatically increase your chance of getting an extreme result.
Notice that the power-law curve starts out below the log-normal one and only passes it at around 100 attempts. With their medians matched, this log-normal puts more weight on moderately large outcomes (it beats 10× about 6% of the time, against 3.5% for the power law), while the power law puts more weight on the truly extreme ones. With only a handful of draws, your best result comes from that middle range, and the less fat-tailed distribution actually serves you better. Only with enough draws do you reach far enough into the tail for the fatter one to pull ahead, and from then on its lead keeps growing. So the number of attempts you can make is not a detail to settle after choosing what to pursue; it helps decide what is worth pursuing. A fat tail pays off only for those who sample it enough times to reach it.
From the perspective of a startup, the number of draws you get is roughly

n \approx \frac{\text{runway}}{\text{time per attempt}} \quad\text{or}\quad \frac{\text{budget}}{\text{cost per attempt}} ,

whichever is smaller. This is the quantitative argument behind the advice to iterate quickly. Halving the cycle time of an experiment doubles the number of draws, and in a fat-tailed world that is worth far more than making each attempt 20% more likely to succeed. For a hardware company, where a prototype cycle can take months, this thought process makes the case for simulation, for renting equipment before buying it, for testing with a mock-up before the real device exists, and for any other trick that turns one expensive draw into several cheap ones.
Two important qualifications to keep in mind: first, draws must be independent to count. Five features built for the same customer on the same assumption are still just one bet. Second, a draw must be a real exposure to the tail. Twenty conversations in which you never ask for money are zero draws from the distribution of sales.

title: 2  Shots on Goal
section: Rule 3: do not truncate your own tail
text:
Rule 3: do not truncate your own tail
Some choices put a ceiling on the possible payout, and so convert a fat-tailed bet into a thin-tailed one, or a convex bet into a concave one, or otherwise reduce the variance you are relying on. Putting in place a ceiling like this can be invisible at the time you accept it. Watch out for these:

A small market. The total addressable market (TAM) is the revenue you would have if every possible customer bought. It is the upper bound of your outcome distribution. A brilliant product in a $20 million market is capped at $20 million.
Exclusivity. Granting your first customer exclusive rights to a field, in exchange for an early contract, sells the tail to pay for the median. If the field is a small part of the total you are going after, maybe geographically or in a particular application, it can be worth it.
Cost-plus pricing. Pricing at cost plus a margin caps what you can earn at a multiple of what you spend. Pricing on the value delivered to the customer does not.
Dependence on your own hours, or another fundamentally limited input. A consulting business is bounded by hours times rate. It can be a fine business, but unless you’ve invented a time machine, it is a thin-tailed one.

None of these is always the wrong choice. Each trades tail for more certainty. If you are going to make that trade, make sure it’s on purpose.

title: 2  Shots on Goal
text:
Rule 4: cap the downside first
The previous three rules assume the downside is limited. Making that true can take work and planning. For example, stage your spending so that no single test can consume the company. Prefer leases to purchases while the direction is uncertain. Keep fixed costs low until you have a tail outcome in sight. Avoid commitments that turn an ordinary disappointment into a fatal one, such as personal guarantees, large minimum order quantities, or customer penalties for late delivery.
There is an asymmetry here that we will develop more in chapter 3. Upside rules are about increasing your expected value. Downside rules are about survival, and survival is a precondition for taking the next draw.

title: 2  Shots on Goal
section: Each draw from a fat-tailed distribution teaches you very little
text:
Each draw from a fat-tailed distribution teaches you very little
So far in this chapter we have been exploring the implications and rules that go with living in a world of fat-tailed outcomes, mainly focused on how to maximize your outcomes. Most of this advice has focused on the structure of how to make a bet. But, you might ask, why not also spend effort making sure that you are taking a draw from a distribution with the best expected value, and avoiding other distributions with a lower chance of success?
To illustrate this, imagine yourself as a VC. You might say: there are so many different early-stage founders making innovative companies with huge potential markets. All of them are good bets, so in order to do better than all of the other VCs out there, you’re only going to invest in the best, most skilled founders.
For the sake of argument, suppose that skill is real and large: a skilled founder increases the median result by 65%, which is a shift of \delta = 0.5 in the mean of the logarithm of the outcome. Suppose outcomes are log-normal with \sigma = 2, which is roughly what the venture data imply. Skill is thus a significant, but not dominant, factor. Suppose also that, by definition, skilled founders are rare, since if everyone were so skilled, then such skill would not produce a shift relative to the typical result. So, say that you are looking for founders who are one in a hundred.
Now design a test. Look at each founder’s track record of n companies, average the logarithms of their outcomes, and flag anyone whose average clears a specified threshold. If the founder is producing outcomes substantially above the mean, that means they must be skilled, right? Not necessarily. Such a test can go wrong in two ways: it can miss a founder who is skilled, but who got unlucky and did not have wildly successful outcomes for other reasons, or it can flag an average founder who happened to get really lucky. Because average founders outnumber skilled ones 99 to 1, this second error is the dangerous one for your goal of identifying skilled founders: even a small false-alarm rate, applied to 99 average founders, produces more flags than the one skilled founder can.
Bayes’ rule makes this precise. The share of flagged founders who are actually skilled is

P(\text{skilled} \mid \text{flagged}) = \frac{0.01 \times \text{power}}{0.01 \times \text{power} + 0.99 \times \text{false-alarm rate}} ,

where the power is the chance that a skilled founder passes the test. In order for P(\text{skilled} \mid \text{flagged}) = 80\%, a skilled founder must be (0.8/0.2) \times 99 = 396 times more likely to pass than an average one. Said another way, your test must be about 400 times more likely to catch a skilled founder than an unskilled one in order for a founder it flags to have only an 80% chance of actually being skilled.
In order to have such a discriminating test, you will need to have a longer track record because the noise in the average shrinks as \sigma/\sqrt{n} while the skill gap \delta stays the same. Measured in standard errors, the separation between the skilled and unskilled founders grows as

\frac{\delta\sqrt{n}}{\sigma} = \frac{\sqrt{n}}{4} .

Instead of getting more data, one way to identify a skilled founder is to set an extreme threshold for your test, since a founder who is consistently producing extreme results is much more likely to be skilled (and also lucky). The tradeoff of this is that you will miss all of the less-lucky but still skilled founders. Since skilled founders are already rare, you don’t want to make this threshold too high, or else you won’t flag anybody at all. Let’s say you want to identify 50% of skilled founders, which would mean you’d expect to find one in every two hundred founders you test. In this case, you can put the threshold at the skilled founders’ expected average. The false-alarm rate is then \Phi(-\sqrt{n}/4), which is the chance that a normally distributed average lands more than \sqrt{n}/4 standard errors above its mean. The requirement 0.5 / \Phi(-\sqrt{n}/4) \ge 396 gives \sqrt{n}/4 \ge 3.02, or

n \approx \left(\frac{3.02\,\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{3.02 \times 2}{0.5}\right)^2 \approx 146 .

In plain language: after watching every founder start 146 companies, this test would identify half of the skilled founders. The other half, who really are skilled, get unlucky often enough that they don’t pass the threshold. And for each founder the test does identify, there is still a 20% chance that they are not actually skilled, just an average founder on a lucky streak. I would not call this an amazing test, but it’s probably good enough to make you a lot of money as a VC.
Of course, in reality, no one starts anything close to 146 companies. At most in a serial entrepreneur’s career you’ll get maybe a handful. This means that, in essentially all cases, no one can discern skill from luck. For any individual founder, including you, a realized outcome is mostly noise around whatever skill is present. This applies to fat-tailed outcomes outside of companies, too. Is the success or failure of an R&D project due to luck, or the skill of researchers? What about the success or failure of your sales team? How well might a potential hire’s resume predict what they would accomplish at your company?
The psychologist Robin Hogarth gave a name to this kind of setting. In a kind learning environment, the rules are stable, similar situations come up again and again, and feedback is fast and accurate. Chess is the classic example: a serious player sees thousands of games, each ends in an unambiguous result within hours, and the rules never change, so experience reliably turns into skill. In a wicked learning environment, feedback is delayed, missing or misleading, and the situations you learn from do not match the ones you will face next. Here experience can confidently teach you the wrong lessons.
Fat tails make an environment wicked almost by construction. The outcomes that dominate the total are, by definition, the ones you see least often, so most of your experience contains little or no information about the events that matter most. You can work for years without ever observing the tail you are trying to learn about. The outcomes you hear about from others have been filtered by survivorship. And in a startup, the result of a decision often arrives years after you made it, mixed together with a particular market, a specific team, and an economy that will not repeat. This means that the 146-company calculation above was actually generous: it assumed every company is a fresh draw from the same distribution, scored promptly and honestly. A real founder gets a handful of slow, noisy draws from different games with rules that keep changing.
None of this means expertise is impossible in wicked domains, but it looks different. It looks less like a chess master’s instant pattern recognition, and more like calibrated judgment, a habit of reaching for base rates and analogies from other fields, and a disciplined process for collecting feedback the environment will not hand you. David Epstein’s Range is the best accessible treatment of how to learn and work in these settings, and I return to some of its specifics in chapter 13, where the question of whether generalists or specialists are better turns largely on how kind or wicked the work is.
The difficulty of distinguishing skill from luck, and of learning in a wicked environment, don’t mean you shouldn’t try. Even a small edge in identifying skill or making better decisions can provide a huge advantage compared to choosing randomly. However, there are several pieces of advice you will want to keep in mind:
Make as much of your work kind as you can. You cannot make starting a company a kind learning environment overall, but a company is built out of many smaller activities, and some of them can be made kind. A sales call typically ends in a yes or a no within weeks or months. A lab experiment gives an answer in days. A hiring decision can be checked against the person’s performance a year later. If you can break slow, large bets into pieces that each return a clear and honest answer quickly, then those pieces can become places where experience compounds into real skill. Doing this takes discipline, because the wicked environment will not do it for you. You have to write down what you expect before you see the result, actually go back and check, and record the misses as carefully as the hits. The feedback in a wicked environment is not only slow and noisy, it is also flattering, because memory quietly edits predictions to fit outcomes. Without a written record kept on purpose, you will learn from your experience only the lessons you already believed.
Judge decisions by their quality, and keep score that way. A good decision is one that looked right given what you could have known and what it cost to know more. Many good decisions lose and many bad ones win. If you only retrospectively reinforce what happened to work based on outcome, you are probably training on noise, and you will also probably bias toward lower-variance situations, which we have shown can actually result in lower expected value. In chapter 9 I describe a way to keep a record of your predictions so you can evaluate the process directly.
Treat advice from winners with care. The founders who give keynote talks were sampled from the far right tail. Whatever they did, hundreds of others did the same and failed, and nobody asked those people for their rules. This is survivorship bias. Prefer explanations that come with a mechanism and a base rate over stories that come with a famous name.
Be humble about your own results, in both directions. A failed company is weak evidence that you are bad at this, and an early success is weak evidence that you are good.






TipKey idea



You cannot control which draw you get. You can control how many independent draws you take, how much each one costs, whether its upside is open and whether its downside is capped.



Lab 2.1: Shots on Goal. Split a fixed budget into bets whose losses are capped. Change the number of bets and the weight of the tail, and watch the distribution of what you take home, including how often a single bet supplies most of it.
A fixed budget is split evenly into n bets. Each bet returns a multiple of its stake drawn from a log-normal distribution with the mean you set and spread \sigma. A bet can lose its stake and no more. The portfolio’s multiple is the average of the n multiples.



Things to try

With the defaults, a single bet has an average multiple of 1.2 and a median far below 1. Set the number of bets to 1 and read the chance of losing money. Then raise it to 30.
Raise \sigma from 1 to 2.5 with the average held fixed. The typical single bet gets worse. What happens to the chance that a 30-bet portfolio doubles?
Look at the share of proceeds from the single best bet. At \sigma = 2 and 30 bets, how much of the portfolio is one company?
Set the average multiple below 1. No number of bets rescues a bet with negative expected value.

title: 3  Don’t Die
text:
Let’s play a game
In chapter 2 we learned why to seek out bets with open upside and to take many of them. That advice has an important condition attached: you have to still be in the game to take the next one. This chapter is all about that condition. We will see how the sizing of your bets is critical to success, and what that means for how you run your company.
Sam Bankman-Fried, hereafter referred to as SBF, has famously said that he would take positive expected value (EV) bets even when the downside is total ruin. In Tyler Cowen’s March 2022 Conversations with Tyler interview, Cowen asked: “Let’s say there’s a game … 51 percent, you double the Earth out somewhere else; 49 percent, it all disappears. Would you play that game?” SBF said yes, and further said that he’d keep playing double-or-nothing. A similar situation came up at SBF’s trial, where Caroline Ellison testified that SBF once posed a coin-flip scenario where if the coin landed on tails, the world would end. But if the coin landed on heads, ‘the world would be twice as good.’ SBF said he would take that bet too. On the face of it, this could seem perfectly rational. If your expected value from a bet is positive, then isn’t it always a good bet to take?
Let’s consider a game with a slightly less extreme coin flip. On heads, your stake grows by 50%. On tails, it shrinks by 40%. The expected change per flip is \tfrac12(+50\%) + \tfrac12(-40\%) = +5\%, so the expected value is clearly positive.
Given that it’s a positive EV as a function of your stake, I invite you to stake your entire wealth, and to do so again every round. The more you bet, the more you should win, right? Not only is the expected value positive, it compounds: after 100 rounds the average wealth across all players is 1.05^{100} \approx 131 times the starting amount. So, wanna play?
The only problem with this game is that it ruins nearly everyone who plays it.
A typical player gets about fifty heads and fifty tails. Each heads-tails pair multiplies wealth by 1.5 \times 0.6 = 0.9, so after 100 rounds the median player has 0.9^{50} \approx 0.5\% of the starting stake. Only about 14% of players are ahead at all. The average of 131 is real, but it is carried by a vanishing sliver of players whose runs of heads made them astronomically rich. Playing this game is a very fat-tailed proposition. Figure 3.1 shows this with 200 players. After 100 rounds their median is 0.005, right where theory puts it, but their average is about 29, less than a quarter of the expected 131, and 83% of that comes from a single player who ended with about 4,800 times the starting stake. Two hundred players are too few to include the even rarer, even luckier ones who hold up the theoretical average.

The dashed line is the expected value, the average over all possible players, which grows 5% a round. The median player loses about 5% a round. 3  Don't Die

title: 3  Don’t Die
text:
Two averages
There are two different ways to average the growth factor of this game.
The ensemble average is taken across many players at one moment: \tfrac12(1.5) + \tfrac12(0.6) = 1.05. This is the arithmetic mean, and it is what “expected value” computes.
The time average is taken along one player’s history. Wealth after T rounds is a product of factors, so its logarithm is a sum. For very long times, the law of large numbers applies and the average growth rate of this sum converges to its expected value. In this single-path case, that average growth rate is the expected logarithm of the factor:

g = \mathbb{E}[\ln(\text{factor})] = \tfrac12 \ln 1.5 + \tfrac12 \ln 0.6 = -0.053 \text{ per round} .

Equivalently, the typical per-round factor is the geometric mean, \sqrt{1.5 \times 0.6} \approx 0.949.
This difference in averages is convex vs. concave bets and Jensen’s inequality from chapter 2 in action. The underlying random variable X is the return on a particular round, 1.5 or 0.6. In order to make a multiplicative return into a sum, we must take the logarithm, so f(X)=\ln(X). In the individual case, we get the expected value of many returns multiplied together, so we must apply the expected value after the logarithm. In the ensemble case, all of the returns apply individually and are then averaged so we can apply the logarithm after the expected value. However, because the logarithm is a concave function, Jensen’s inequality works against us, and more variance results in a worse outcome:
\mathbb{E}[\ln(X)] < \ln(\mathbb{E}[X])  with the difference becoming larger with more variance in X. Go back to SBF’s coin flips, where he is willing to bet everything on a 51% chance of a 100% gain. The expected value of this is 51\%-49\%=2\%, which is positive, so he takes it. But the expected value of the logarithms is
51\% \times \ln(2) + 49\% \times \ln(0)=0.35 - \infty=-\infty which is a better expression of what to expect as an individual taking this bet, rather than taking this bet many times in parallel in a portfolio. So, would you take it?
A system in which the time average equals the ensemble average is called ergodic, which you may have encountered as a standard assumption in a statistical mechanics course. As we have just seen, multiplicative wealth is not ergodic: the ensemble average says +5% a round while the time average says −5%. The physicist Ole Peters has argued that much confusion in economics comes from using the ensemble average where the time average is the relevant one. For example, insurance can look like a zero-sum game, where the insurer wins and the person buying insurance loses. But viewed through the time average, it can be win-win: the buyer gives up a little expected value to remove a large multiplicative loss, which raises their long-run growth rate, while the insurer, being much larger, absorbs the risk with little effect on its own growth.
Now think about you and your investor. Your investor, who has a portfolio of thirty companies where each is a small share of the fund, experiences something closer to the ensemble average. You, as founder, hold one company, essentially compounding your results over time along a single path. The same bet (your company) is thus evaluated with different mathematics by the two people at the table. When an investor says “you should take that risk” and you feel reluctant, it is quite possible that both of you are computing the exact same risk and reward, but looking at it from different perspectives.

title: 3  Don’t Die
section: How much to stake: the Kelly criterion
text:
How much to stake: the Kelly criterion
The coin game is not bad in itself; it is bad when you stake your entire wealth every time. Suppose you stake only a fraction f of your wealth each round and keep the rest in reserve. If a win pays b per unit staked with probability p, and a loss costs a per unit staked with probability q = 1 - p, the long-run growth rate is

g(f) = p \ln(1 + b f) + q \ln(1 - a f) .

Setting the derivative to zero gives the stake that maximizes long-run growth, known as the Kelly criterion after John Kelly of Bell Labs:

f^{*} = \frac{p}{a} - \frac{q}{b} .

For the coin game f^* = 0.5/0.4 - 0.5/0.5 = 25\%.








Figure 3.2: Long-run growth rate of the coin game as a function of the fraction staked. Growth peaks at a 25% stake, is zero again at 50%, and is negative beyond that.



Figure 3.2 shows three significant features that carry over to real decisions:
There is an interior optimum. Staking nothing earns nothing, staking everything loses, and the best stake lies in between. The favorable odds are a reason to bet anything at all. The variance is the reason to keep most of your wealth out of any single round.
Overbetting is far worse than underbetting. The curve is nearly flat to the left of the peak and steep to the right. Staking half the optimum amount gives up only a quarter of the growth. Staking twice the optimum reduces growth to zero. Anything beyond twice the optimum turns a favorable game into a losing one. Since in real life you pretty much never know the true odds, you’re not going to be able to calculate the optimal amount to bet with 100% certainty. Given that you will probably be wrong, it is far better to err toward a smaller stake. Professional gamblers call this “half Kelly.”
The right size to bet is roughly the edge divided by the variance. For small bets the formula reduces to f^* \approx \text{edge}/\text{variance}, where edge is that positive EV. A bet with a modest edge and a huge variance deserves a small stake, however exciting its expected value. One wonders if knowing this simple formula could have saved SBF a lot of grief.

Lab 3.1: Size the Bet. Each round deals a coin game with its own odds, gain and loss. Choose the fraction of your wealth to stake on every flip, lock it in, and see how close you came to the Kelly stake. Play a few rounds before you peek at the hints.
You stake a fraction f of your current wealth on every flip. Heads, with probability p, adds b per dollar staked; tails removes a. Your score is the share of the best possible long-run growth rate g(f) = p\ln(1 + bf) + q\ln(1 - af) that your stake achieves, where the best is reached at f^* = p/a - q/b. Some games have a negative edge; the right answer to those is not to play.



Things to try

Play five rounds on instinct, then turn on the hints and play five more. Does edge ÷ variance get you closer?
After locking in, drag the slider to half the Kelly stake and then to twice it, and compare the growth at each. Which mistake costs more?
Find a game with a big payout on heads but a low chance of heads. How does the Kelly stake compare with what felt right?
Watch the single-run chart for a game where you overbet. Sometimes the overbet path is ahead for a while. Why doesn’t that make it the better choice?

title: 3  Don’t Die
section: What a founder can do with this
text:
What a founder can do with this
A founder cannot put 25% of themselves into a company. Your time, your reputation, and sometimes your savings are all in. However, being all-in doesn’t have to mean being totally out of the game if you lose. In Walter Isaacson’s 2023 biography, Elon Musk, he recounts a story shared by Max Levchin, Musk’s PayPal co-founder. Levchin recalls a high-stakes Texas Hold ’Em game at a friend’s bachelor pad, where Musk joined even though he wasn’t a card player. In Levchin’s words: “Elon just proceeded to go all in on every hand and lose. Then he would buy more chips and double down. Eventually, after losing many hands, he went all in and won. Then he said, ‘Right, fine, I’m done.’” In one sense, Musk was going all in. In another, he was actually staking a very small amount of his total wealth, and could easily buy back in when he lost. For your startup journey, being all in on your time and effort doesn’t necessarily mean you won’t have more time and effort to keep betting with if your company fails.
The sizing rule also applies one level down, to the bets you and the company make day to day. You can think of your company as a sequence of bets: this product, this customer segment, this hire, this production run. Each one stakes some fraction of your available resources. The Kelly sizing logic tells you the following:

Never stake the whole company on one roll. A single experiment that consumes the remaining runway is a full-stake coin game, whatever its expected value. Commit in stages. A smaller test or prototype that costs a fifth of the time and money while answering most of the question is nearly always available.
Reserves are productive. Cash that is not staked is what lets you play the next round. Treat a request to “put the money to work faster” with the suspicion it deserves.
Remove small recurring chances of ruin. If some practice carries a 1% chance per month of ending the company (a single supplier with no alternative, an unprotected safety hazard, one person who alone knows how the process works), the chance of surviving three years of it is only 0.99^{36} \approx 70\%. Suddenly what you might have thought of as a 1% tail risk becomes a significant 30% risk over time. Risks that repeat are much larger than they appear at first glance.
Size your personal stake too. A founder who has also mortgaged the house and gone without salary for two years is at full Kelly on top of full Kelly. The same goes for working yourself to the point of exhaustion. Paying yourself enough to live on and working at a sustainable level is risk management for the company, and for yourself. Also consider lowering your personal stake with a secondary sale in an earlier round of financing. Getting a meaningful amount of money for yourself personally can actually help align you with your investors’ incentives by lowering your effective stake and thus making higher variance more appealing.

None of this is an argument for timidity. Chapter 2’s lessons still apply: take every cheap convex bet you can find. The lesson from Kelly is about choosing the right size for each of these bets.

title: 3  Don’t Die
text:
Runway is a random walk
The standard way to calculate runway is to divide cash by monthly burn. With $1.8 million in the bank and a burn of $100,000 a month, the spreadsheet says 18 months.
Real cash flows fluctuate. Customers pay late, a tool breaks, a purchase order slips a quarter. You can account for this by modeling the cash balance as a random walk: each month it changes by a drift \mu plus a random term with standard deviation \sigma. Running out of money, meaning you hit zero, functions as an absorbing barrier: a walk that touches zero stops there. For a company that is losing money on average (\mu < 0), the time to reach zero from a starting balance C_0 has

\text{mean} = \frac{C_0}{|\mu|}, \qquad \text{standard deviation} = \frac{\sigma \sqrt{C_0}}{|\mu|^{3/2}} .









Figure 3.3: Month in which the cash runs out for a company with $1.8 million and an average burn of $100,000 a month. With modest month-to-month variation the answer is 18 months give or take two or three. With lumpy cash flows, a quarter of the simulated companies are out of money by month 14.



With \sigma = \$60{,}000 per month, the formula gives a standard deviation of about 2.5 months in the time to reach zero. In simulations, one company in ten is out of cash by month 15, three months before the simple calculation indicated running out of money. With \sigma = \$150{,}000, which is plausible when revenue arrives in a few large payments, the standard deviation is more than six months. In simulations, a quarter of the companies are out by month 14, and one in twenty is out by month 11. That’s a whole seven months before you might have been expecting to hit zero. If you were trying to be safe and plan a six-month buffer for fundraising, there’s a not insignificant chance you are forced to start well before you planned to.
Raising money takes time, commonly several months, but that time has a long tail of its own. Presumably you will be watching your runway and will start your raise when you think you have a comfortable amount of time before going bankrupt. However, you probably also have in mind some clear milestones that you want to hit in order to be in a good position to raise, and that takes time to achieve. The implication is that if you plan all of these timelines around the mean, you are accepting even odds of running out early. Think about your runway, time to raise, and time to hit milestones as distributions, and then act based on a reasonably pessimistic assumption. Remember that going all-in and losing can work out long-term if you can keep buying back in, but if you bet everything and hit zero, that’s it.

Profitable on average is not the same as safe
Paul Graham’s test for a young company is whether it is default alive: on its current trajectory, does it reach profitability before the money runs out? Even for a narrowly profitable company, a random walk suggests danger. If the drift is positive, the probability of ever touching zero from a starting balance C_0 is

\Pr(\text{ruin}) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{2 \mu C_0}{\sigma^2}\right) .

Take a hypothetical company earning $20,000 a month on average, with monthly swings of $150,000 and a cash balance of $500,000 in the bank. The exponent is 2 \times 20 \times 500 / 150^2 = 0.89, so the probability of ruin is 41%. This company is profitable and has more than two years of average profit in reserve, and yet its survival is still close to a coin flip. The dependence on the starting balance is exponential, so tripling the reserve to $1.5 million brings the risk down to 7%, almost a sixfold reduction.
Solving for the reserve that holds the risk of ruin to a chosen level gives

C_0 = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\mu} \ln\frac{1}{\Pr(\text{ruin})} .

The reserve you need grows with the square of the volatility of your cash flow and inversely with your margin. Smoothing lumpy cash flows (deposits, milestone payments, more and smaller customers) is worth far more than simply trying to increase profitability. Conversely, variability in cash flow has a real cost in terms of the reserves you need as a cushion.

title: 3  Don’t Die
text:
Survival first, then expected value
We can summarize the takeaways from this chapter as:

Along a single path, the quantity to maximize is the long-run growth rate, which is the expected value of the logarithm. This quantity penalizes variance, and it treats ruin as infinitely bad.
Positive expected value is necessary for a good bet. It is not sufficient. The size of the stake relative to your reserves decides whether a good bet is good for you. Keep this in mind, and stay out of prison, and you’re already doing better than SBF.
Runway is a distribution. Plan to its pessimistic tail, and remember that the reserve needed for safety scales with variance squared. Reducing variability has concrete value.







TipKey idea



Take every favorable, capped bet you can find, and size each one so that a run of losses still leaves you in the game.



Lab 3.2: Runway Random Walk. Set starting cash, burn, revenue growth and month-to-month volatility. The lab simulates cash paths and reports the probability of running out before break-even, along with the percentiles of the date.
Revenue starts at today’s level and grows exponentially at a rate that is uncertain: each simulated company draws its own growth rate. Cash changes each month by revenue minus expenses, plus a random swing. A path ends when the cash reaches zero or when revenue reaches expenses.



Things to try

Compare the spreadsheet runway with the month by which one company in ten has run out.
Set the growth uncertainty to zero, then to ±6%. The average growth is the same. What happens to the chance of running out?
Halve the month-to-month swing. How much extra cash would buy the same reduction in risk?
Find the lowest growth rate at which nine companies in ten reach break-even with the default cash.
